papers.title_in_file: Innovative Approaches to Teaching Quantum Computer Programming and Quantum Software Engineering
papers.what_it_is: A short curriculum proposal from Finnish and Spanish lecturers for teaching quantum programming with Docker, Qiskit, PennyLane and Ocean SDK.

assertions.value: The authors propose a six-step teaching approach for quantum computer programming and quantum software engineering, with practical teaching of Qiskit, PennyLane and Ocean.
quotes: This paper proposes a six-step teaching approach for teaching quantum computer programming and quantum software engineering
Our emphasis during this course is practical teaching of three frameworks: Qiskit from IBM [1], PennyLane from Xanadu [5], and Ocean from D-Wave [6].
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own scope in Section I, p.1.

assertions.value: The authors state that, to the best of their knowledge, their curriculum structure is distinct from most existing courses, and that they have not found another course covering all three of these SDKs.
quotes: To the best of our knowledge, our curriculum structure is distinct from most existing courses.
We have yet to encounter a course on quantum computer programming that offers and discusses three different SDKs: D-Wave, Qiskit, and PennyLane.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim with no survey of other courses in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: No comparison against other curricula is presented, so the uniqueness statement is untested in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the curriculum has not yet been evaluated with students: a questionnaire and an empirical evaluation are planned future work.
quotes: Next on our agenda, we intend to distribute a questionnaire and, using the students' evaluations, present our findings.
Additionally, we plan to conduct an empirical evaluation and publish the preliminary results.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this limit in Section VIII-C, Future Works.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper offers no outcome data on teaching effectiveness.

papers.title_in_file: Construction of Chemistry Inspired Dynamic Ansatz Utilizing Generative Machine Learning
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Theory discussion of limitations (sections II), Results (hyperparameters, comparisons, convergence), Conclusions; skipped the derivation details and supporting information.
papers.what_it_is: A method that uses a Restricted Boltzmann Machine and perturbative screening to build a shallow-depth VQE ansatz for molecular ground-state energies.

assertions.value: The authors report that the RBM1s-dUCCSDTS ansatz reaches an energy accuracy close to dUCCSDT (a numeric bound is given in the text and Fig. 3) while using a substantially shallower ansatz.
assertions.anchor: Section III, Results, comparison of convergence and Fig. 3, pp.7-8
quotes: This accuracy is achieved using a substantially shallow depth ansatz (see Fig. 3).
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on a few small molecules.
assertions.reader_inference: The comparison is against a classical-reference ansatz, not against experimental data or hardware.

assertions.value: The authors state that all calculations used an STO-3G basis, the RBM was trained using 10000 determinants, and the molecules studied in the accuracy figure are BH, H2O and CH2.
assertions.anchor: Section III, Results, computational details and Fig. 3, p.7
quotes: All the subsequent calculations have been performed using an STO-3G basis.
The RBM has been trained using 10000 determinants.
Energy accuracy for (a) BH, (b) H2O and (c) CH2.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own computational setup in Section III.

assertions.value: The authors state that the RBM's ability to generate higher-rank determinants may be limited if the primary excitation subspace does not capture enough correlation patterns, and that the accuracy of the ansatz depends strongly on the starting parameters of the variational optimization.
assertions.anchor: Section II discussion and Section IV, Conclusions, pp.6-9
quotes: may be limited if the primary excitation subspace fails to capture sufficient correlation patterns.
The accuracy of the developed ansatz is highly dependent on the starting parameters of the variational optimization.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state these limits in Section II and the Conclusions.

papers.title_in_file: EnQode: Fast Amplitude Embedding for Quantum Machine Learning Using Classical Data
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Methodology overview, Evaluation setup and results, Conclusion; skipped background and related-work detail.
papers.what_it_is: A cluster-based approximate amplitude-embedding method with a fixed low-depth hardware-tailored ansatz, evaluated in simulation against exact embedding.

assertions.value: The authors report that in noisy IBM hardware simulation EnQode reaches a state fidelity more than 14 times that of the exact-embedding Baseline, and a circuit depth more than 28 times lower.
assertions.anchor: Section I, Introduction, p.1; Section VI-B, Fig. 8(b)
quotes: In noisy IBM quantum hardware simulation settings, EnQode demonstrates a state fidelity improvement of over 14
Compared to the Baseline, EnQode reduces the circuit depth by over 28
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation result from one study; noisy simulation based on the ibm_brisbane device model.
assertions.reader_inference: The multipliers are relative to exact amplitude embedding transpiled at optimization level 0; they measure state fidelity, not downstream model accuracy.

assertions.value: The authors report that EnQode reaches an average state fidelity of 89% in ideal simulation when transpiled to real hardware, which is lower than the Baseline's exact embedding.
quotes: In ideal simulations (Fig. 8(a)), EnQode achieves an average state fidelity of 89% when transpiled to real hardware
Although EnQode has worse fidelity compared to Baseline in ideal simulation
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract's 'over 90% fidelity' differs from this 89% average, so the headline figure depends on which samples or setting is meant.

assertions.value: The authors state the evaluation used 8-qubit circuits with an 8-layer ansatz, simulated density matrices modeled on ibm_brisbane, and samples from MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR10 with 5 classes per dataset and 500 images per class.
quotes: For all experiments, we used 8-qubit circuits, with an 8-layer ansatz structure as depicted in Fig. 2.
We randomly sampled 5 classes for each dataset, and for each class, we randomly sampled 500 images from that class.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own evaluation setup in Section V.
assertions.reader_inference: All reported results are simulation of 8-qubit circuits; no run on physical hardware or end-to-end classifier accuracy is reported in the sections read.

papers.title_in_file: A Survey on Applications of Quantum Computing for Unit Commitment
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Section II overview, start of Section III, and Section IV Conclusion; did not read every per-paper review in Section III.
papers.what_it_is: A survey of annealing, variational, quantum machine learning and quantum-inspired approaches to the power-system unit commitment problem.

assertions.value: The authors state that the paper is a survey of research on quantum computing for the unit commitment problem, categorized by annealing-based, variational hybrid, quantum machine learning and quantum-inspired methods.
quotes: This paper presents a comprehensive survey of existing research on the applications of quantum computing for solving the UC problem.
The reviewed works are categorized based on the employed quantum paradigms, including annealing-based, variational hybrid, quantum machine learning, and quantum-inspired methods.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own scope in the Abstract.

assertions.value: The authors state, as a conclusion of the survey, that quantum hardware has limited qubits, noise and restricted connectivity, and that unit commitment constraints lead to large, tightly coupled QUBOs that are hard for NISQ devices.
assertions.anchor: Section IV, Conclusion and Future Works
quotes: Quantum hardware has limited qubits, noise, and restricted connectivity.
UC constraints lead to large and tightly coupled QUBOs that are hard for NISQ devices.
assertions.certainty_reason: A survey synthesis of other studies; no new experiment in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum neural network and quantum reinforcement learning models require long training and lack strong reliability guarantees for large unit commitment cases, and that quantum-inspired methods do not provide true quantum speedup.
assertions.anchor: Section IV, Conclusion and Future Works
quotes: QNN and QRL models require long training and lack strong reliability guarantees for large UC cases.
Quantum-inspired methods do not provide true quantum speedup and may struggle with large time horizons.
assertions.certainty_reason: A survey synthesis of other studies; no new experiment in this paper.

papers.title_in_file: Two-stage Distributed Variational Quantum Eigensolver Software for QUBO and Quadratic Programming
papers.version_note: File is arXiv v3 (2 Jul 2026) titled 'Two-stage Distributed Variational Quantum Eigensolver Software for QUBO and Quadratic Programming'; the filename carries the earlier 'Distributed Implementation of Variational Quantum Eigensolver' title.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, software overview, Section 4.0.1 ablation and 4.0.2 start, Conclusion; skipped the QQP derivations, API detail and large-scale QQP experiment.
papers.what_it_is: Open-source software for a distributed variational quantum eigensolver with metaheuristic warm starts for QUBO, plus a QP-to-QUBO reformulation (QQP).

assertions.value: The authors report that over 80 random QUBO instances the distributed DVQE with Black Hole warm start solved 66 out of 80 exactly (82.5%), against 44 out of 80 (55.0%) for the monolithic random-initialization baseline.
assertions.anchor: Section 4.0.1, Ablation Study on DVQE, Table 1, pp.19-20
quotes: The D-BH variant solves 66 out of 80 instances exactly, corresponding to a success rate of 82.5%.
The monolithic random baseline solved 44 out of 80 instances exactly, giving a success rate of 55.0%.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on simulated circuits.
assertions.reader_inference: The instances reach at most 18 variables per the text read, so the result is for small problems.

assertions.value: The authors report that the distributed random-initialization variant solved 42 out of 80 instances exactly (52.5%), which they read as showing that the distributed implementation preserves the behavior of the monolithic solver.
quotes: The distributed random variant solved 42 out of 80 instances exactly, giving a success rate of 52.5%.
These two results are close, which indicates that the distributed implementation preserves the behavior of the monolithic DVQE solver under the same random initialization setting.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on simulated circuits.

assertions.value: The authors state that the work does not claim quantum speedup because the experiments run on CPU-based quantum-circuit software, and that the DVQE uses Qiskit Aer as its simulation backend.
assertions.anchor: Section 1 contributions and Section 5, Conclusion, p.23
quotes: This work does not claim quantum speedup, since the experiments are performed using a CPU-based quantum-circuit software.
A distributed variational quantum eigensolver (DVQE) is developed with an open-source software for solving QUBO problems using Qiskit Aer as the quantum-circuit simulation backend.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this limit in the Conclusion, p.23.

papers.title_in_file: A quantum-enhanced support vector machine for galaxy classification
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Results (training-size comparison, device run), Discussion on quantum advantage, Conclusions; skipped the data-preparation and kernel derivation detail.
papers.what_it_is: A quantum-kernel SVM for classifying elliptical and spiral galaxies, run in simulation and on a small IBM device.

assertions.value: The authors report that the quantum-kernel and classical-kernel SVMs reached the same ROC AUC of 0.946 with 40k training points and 10k test points, and that the two classifiers have comparable performance regardless of training size.
quotes: The scores derived for the Kgal
A ROC AUC score of 0.946
We utilised 40k data points to train the classifiers, a number constrained by the computational resources available for running the quantum kernel classifier.
Additionally, 10k datapoints were allocated for testing.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study; quantum kernel was computed in noiseless simulation.
assertions.reader_inference: Parity with a classical kernel is not an advantage result.

assertions.value: The authors report that on the 5-qubit ibmq_manila device, with error suppression and mitigation, the SVM performance agreed with simulation within the uncertainties on a small dataset, and caution that this may not extend to much larger datasets.
assertions.anchor: Section 4, quantum device run, Table 2, p.5-6
quotes: This device consists of 5 qubits which are positioned in a line
The performance of the simulation and quantum device agree within the uncertainties.
Therefore, the similarity between simulation and quantum device is not necessarily extendible to much larger datasets.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on a very small dataset.

assertions.value: The authors state that whether a quantum advantage in kernel computation is practically achievable is an open question, and describe their study as a proof-of-concept.
quotes: Whether or not a quantum advantage in kernel computation is practically achievable is yet an open question
Our study serves as a proof-of-concept
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this limit in Section 5, p.6.

papers.title_in_file: QGAN-based data augmentation for hybrid quantum-classical neural networks
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Method overview, Experiment setup and results discussion, Conclusion; skipped related-work and some experiment detail.
papers.what_it_is: A data augmentation framework that uses a quantum GAN to enlarge training data for a hybrid quantum-classical neural network, tested in simulation on three MNIST digits.

assertions.value: The authors report that the QGAN slightly underperforms DCGAN at 500 iterations but surpasses it at 200 iterations (84% vs. 82%) using a shallower network and half the parameters.
quotes: Although QGAN slightly underperforms DCGAN at 500 iterations, it surpasses DCGAN at 200 iterations (84% vs. 82%) using a shallower network and half the parameters.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one simulation study on a small task.
assertions.reader_inference: A two-point difference on a 3-class, 100-sample-per-class task is small and no variance is quoted in the text read.

assertions.value: The authors report that, compared with GAN-1 and GAN-2, the QGAN improved classification accuracy on MNIST by 6.3 and 3 percentage points respectively.
quotes: Compared with GAN-1 (similar structure and parameters) and GAN-2 (more complex architecture), QGAN improved classification accuracy on MNIST by 6.3 and 3 percentage points, respectively
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one simulation study.

assertions.value: The authors state that, because of simulation cost, the MNIST task was reduced to a three-class problem and only 100 samples per class were used for training and testing.
quotes: Due to the high computational cost of simulating large-scale quantum systems, the MNIST task is simplified to a three-class problem
To simulate real-world data scarcity, only 100 samples per class are used for training and testing, significantly reducing data size.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental scope in Section 4.
assertions.reader_inference: Results are from simulation on a three-class subset, so they do not show behavior on full MNIST or on hardware.

assertions.value: The authors state in the abstract that quantum neural networks converge faster and achieve higher accuracy than classical models.
quotes: Quantum neural networks converge faster and achieve higher accuracy than classical models.
assertions.certainty_reason: A general statement with no supporting evidence in the paper's own experiments.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper's experiments compare generators for augmentation; they do not test this general statement.

quotes: In this position paper, we argue that while real-world NISQ quantum applications have yet to surpass their classical counterparts
We have identified three key strategies to guide NISQ computing towards practical and useful implementations.

assertions.value: The authors state that real-world NISQ quantum applications have yet to surpass their classical counterparts.
quotes: real-world NISQ quantum applications have yet to surpass their classical counterparts
